pairs.reply1:
He uses it as an example that computers don't have to be digital Turing machines. The earliest computers, he says, were analogue devices that worked in continuous time, and the Antikythera mechanism is his "excellent example" [spya-zg9me8]. The point sits in the "Other games in town" section. There he argues that Turing-style algorithms (step-by-step rules that turn one string of symbols into another) are only one kind of computation. Biological systems are full of continuous and random dynamics, so it is "presumptuous" to assume only Turing computation matters for consciousness [spya-n393ru]. The example is a short historical aside. It supports his claim that broader kinds of computation exist and are more tied to their physical material than digital computing is [spya-gamzr3 spya-kjfjgm].

The article gives the date as "around 2,000 BCE" [spya-zg9me8]. That looks like a slip. [World History Encyclopedia](https://www.worldhistory.org/Antikythera_Mechanism/) dates the device to roughly 205–60 BCE, and [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antikythera_mechanism) says it was made in the 2nd century BC. "About 2,000 years ago" is probably what was meant. This doesn't affect his argument.
pairs.reply2:
He uses it as an early example of computation that isn't digital Turing computation. The article says the earliest computers were analogue devices working in continuous time, not digital Turing machines. The Antikythera mechanism is its first illustration, and the article follows it with cybernetics in the 1950s.

The example sits in the "Other Games In Town" section. That section argues that Turing algorithms are powerful, but many kinds of dynamics and functions go beyond them. The mechanism is a reminder that "computation" has not always meant Turing-style algorithms. This sets up the point that alternative forms of computation are more closely tied to their material basis, and so less substrate-flexible, than standard digital computation. That supports the essay's wider case against computational functionalism, the view that the right computation is enough for consciousness.

The article dates the mechanism to around 2,000 BCE. The article doesn't say so, but my recollection is that it is usually dated to roughly the second century BCE. I haven't verified that, so check it before relying on either date. The date doesn't affect the argument.

articleBlocks.text: This reveals the weakness of the popular “neural replacement” thought experiment, most commonly associated with Chalmers, which invites us to imagine progressively replacing brain parts with silicon equivalents that function in exactly the same way as their biological counterparts. The supposed conclusion is that properties like cognition and consciousness must be substrate independent (or at least silicon-substrate-flexible). This thought experiment has become a prominent trope in discussions of artificial consciousness, usually invoked to support its possibility. pairs.reply1:
Seth says the thought experiment fails at the start, because its central premise can't be met. The experiment asks us to imagine swapping brain parts one by one for silicon parts that behave identically, and concludes that consciousness must be substrate independent. Seth calls it a popular trope, mentions that Hinton used it to claim conscious AI is already here, and says it "fails at its first hurdle" because a perfect silicon replacement for any part of the brain is impossible [spya-ahtr6e].

His reasoning comes just before that. Real brains are tightly integrated across scales, which he links to "generative entrenchment." So you can't assume a single neuron can be swapped for a silicon equivalent that keeps its input-output behavior exactly the same [spya-jnwfxp]. His example is work by Chintaluri and Vogels, who found that some neurons fire spikes apparently to clear metabolic waste. Replacing those neurons would mean building a silicon metabolism too, and he says silicon isn't suited to that [spya-un9fjn].

In the argument as a whole, this is a consequence of his first claim, that brains are not computers, which he builds around the missing split between "what they do" and "what they are" [spya-zw2m7u]. The thought experiment needs that split, which is why he uses the point against it.

The article doesn't say how Chalmers or others would answer. My inference is that a defender could treat the experiment as an idealization, which would shift the dispute to whether the replacement is possible in principle. Seth's text only argues it is impossible in practice.

Seth thinks the thought experiment fails because its starting premise can't be met. He says it "fails at its first hurdle," since no part of the brain could be swapped for a perfect silicon equivalent [spya-ahtr6e]. In the same passage he describes the experiment as asking us to replace brain parts step by step with silicon parts that work identically. The supposed conclusion is that cognition and consciousness don't depend on what the brain is made of. He also notes that Hinton recently used it to argue conscious AI is already here [spya-ahtr6e].

His reason comes just before. Real brains are tightly integrated across scales, which he calls "generative entrenchment." So you can't assume a single neuron could be replaced by a silicon one while keeping its input-output behavior exactly the same [spya-jnwfxp]. His example is work by Chintaluri and Vogels, who found that some neurons fire spikes apparently to clear metabolic waste. A perfect silicon stand-in would need its own silicon-based metabolism, which he says silicon isn't suited for [spya-un9fjn].

My inference is that he isn't saying the reasoning is invalid. The experiment assumes the replacement preserves function perfectly, and he denies that this can happen. This also ties to his first argument, that brains aren't computers because what they do can't be separated from what they are [spya-zw2m7u].

articleBlocks.text: At around the same time that Turing was making his mark, the mathematician Walter Pitts and neurophysiologist Warren McCulloch showed, in a landmark paper, that networks of highly simplified abstract neurons can perform logical operations (Figure 2). Later work, by the logician Stephen Kleene among others, demonstrated that artificial neural networks like these, when provided with a tape-like memory (as in the Turing machine), were “Turing complete” — that they could, in principle, implement any Turing machine, any algorithm.

pairs.facts: Nothing in this passage is known to be wrong or seriously disputed; McCulloch & Pitts 1943; Nagel 1974 'What is it like to be a bat?'.
pairs.reply1:
He says McCulloch and Pitts showed in a landmark paper that networks of highly simplified abstract neurons can perform logical operations [spya-va8qxr]. The claim that such networks could in principle run any algorithm comes from later work, by Kleene among others. That work showed the networks were "Turing complete" once given a tape-like memory, as in a Turing machine [spya-va8qxr]. So the "any algorithm" result isn't credited to McCulloch and Pitts themselves. Figure 2's caption shows what their simplified neuron does: it sums weighted inputs and outputs a 1 or a 0 [spya-qknqjx].

Seth uses this to set up his first argument, that brains are not computers. He pairs the result with Turing's work and calls the pair a "mathematical marriage of convenience." You can treat brains as simple networks and ignore their messy biology, and in return you get everything Turing computation offers [spya-v5vz2t]. Today's artificial neural networks are the "children" of that marriage [spya-va72zk].

He then argues the marriage "starts to fall apart" if what brains do can't be separated from what they physically are [spya-p4vmm0]. The McCulloch-Pitts result is therefore the foundation he is arguing against, not a point he disputes.
pairs.reply2:
He says McCulloch and Pitts showed, in a landmark paper, that networks of highly simplified abstract neurons can perform logical operations. The "Turing complete" part came later, and he credits it to Kleene and others, not to McCulloch and Pitts. Given a tape-like memory, as in the Turing machine, such networks could in principle implement any algorithm.

The Figure 2 caption describes the original neuron. It summed weighted inputs and gave an output of 1 if the sum passed a fixed threshold, and 0 if it didn't.

In the argument, this result is one half of what he calls a "mathematical marriage of convenience". It lets you ignore the messy neurobiological reality of real brains and still get everything Turing computation offers. He sets it up so that the next paragraphs can attack it. He says today's artificial neural networks are direct descendants of McCulloch, Pitts and Kleene. He then argues that real brains have no sharp separation between "mindware" and "wetware".

input.said: He says consciousness is about being rather than doing, and he uses Nagel's line, that something's conscious if there's something it is like to be it.

articleBlocks.text: Consciousness, in contrast to intelligence, is mostly about being. Half a century ago, the philosopher Thomas Nagel famously offered that “an organism has conscious mental states if and only if there is something it is like to be that organism.” Consciousness is the difference between normal wakefulness and the oblivion of deep general anesthesia. It is the experiential aspect of brain function and especially of perception: the colors, shapes, tastes, emotions, thoughts and more, that give our lives texture and meaning. The blueness of the sky on a clear day. The bitter tang and headrush of your first coffee.
